newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Rouble looks robust as capital may return.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Rouble looks robust as capital may return.

text.p: The Russian rouble is likely to remain under mild pressure to appreciate in the near future as the country's improving economic and political outlook brings in more funds from abroad, analysts say.
The pressure on the rouble, moving within a tightly mapped pre-announced corridor, may further increase if capital that has left Russia in recent years begins to return, they said.
"So far the foreign inflow is not overwhelming but if (Russian) capital returns, stronger appreciation pressure may arise," said Professor Stanislaw Gomulka of the London School of Economics.

Economists estimate that some $60 billion have been siphoned out of Russia since reforms there started. But in a sign of growing confidence, the capital flight seems to be over and some analysts believe money has already started to return.

Although expectations of economic recovery this year seem unlikely to materialise, growth looks set to come next year, while investors are heartened by signs of growing fiscal and macroeconomic stability.
"Stabilisation in Russia is remarkably successful," said David Lubin, emerging markets economist at HSBC Markets.
"And the biggest change is that the capital flight stopped."
MONEY SUPPLY GROWS ON FOREIGN INFLOWS

A rapid growth in inflows may pose a monetary problem and slow the fall in inflation, analysts say. So far, excess money from abroad has been soaked up in financial assets, but next year is a bit of a mystery, they said.
Demand for Russian securities is reflected in a fall in Treasury bill yields to record lows below 19 percent, and recent record highs in share prices.
Apart from a heavy currency inflow due to the government's foreign revenue, pressure on big debtors such as gas monopoly Gazprom to pay taxes has also boosted demand for roubles.
"Issuing Eurobonds, and big sales of currency earnings by Gazprom are real financial instruments; it is not just printing money," said CS First Boston vice-president Sergey Koshelenko.
"Meanwhile the central bank and finance ministry have used non-inflationary methods to build up money supply and I don't think this will bring about a surge in inflation."

The central bank has been a net buyer of foreign currency for several months, pushing up its reserves, as Russian investors show willingness to hold rouble assets again. Net international reserves nearly tripled in May and June to $11 billion.

The result is seen in a three percent decline in the rouble against the dollar on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) in the first half of this year, while inflation over the same period was 8.6 percent.
NO PLANS IN SIGHT TO LIBERALISE CURRENCY REGIME
The exchange rate is one of Russia's main anchors against inflation. The central bank announces a series of daily bands for the rouble every six months or year.
Within that range, every morning the central bank sets a narrow bid/offer spread for deals with major banks, which effectively limits the rouble in the interbank market.
The tightly controlled rouble has never strayed outside the daily bands, and has only occasionally moved a few points outside the daily central bank spread, grazing the upper limit.
Market confidence in the central bank's ability to hold the line is reflected in current forward rates.
December rouble forwards are quoted at 5,920/23 per dollar and January forwards at 5,948/51 -- in the upper half of the 5,750-6,350 corridor for December 31.

The strictly regulated corridor system and closed Russian market means Russia is for now immune to the speculative attacks but there is increasing concern that as more and more hot money flows into the country, a rapid pullout may cause a currency crisis in a few years' time.

Officials show no signs of abandoning the corridor system for, say, a floating rouble, and central bank chairman Sergei Dubinin has ruled out any "dramatic changes, either in technical management, or in currency and monetary policy" for 1998.
INFLATION OUTLOOK IS AMBIGUOUS

But reluctance to allow the rouble, which is seen as undervalued, to rise faster forces the central bank to buy currencies from banks, which boosts money supply. Its growth had already outstripped inflation in the first five months of this year.

On July 1 M2 money supply was 363.8 trillion roubles ($63 billion), up 23.2 percent from January 1, while consumer prices rose 8.6 percent over the same period. Total reserves, including gold, reached over $23 billion in June from almost $17 billion in March and are likely to keep growing. The government has also raised billions of dollars abroad from Eurobonds and World Bank and International Monetary Fund loans.
To offset the monetary expansion, the central bank has been selling government securities from its portfolio in June and July.

The central bank's first deputy chairman Sergei Aleksashenko said the markets had already digested these funds without stability suffering, as evidenced by steady T-bill prices and overnight rouble rates near zero.

But some inflationary impact could not be ruled out, he acknowledged. The government was raising these funds partly to pay off pension and wage arrears, and once this money is transferred it could be used to buy consumer goods.
"As far as the consumer market is concerned, the question is a little more complex," Aleksashenko said. "When people get a lot of money then prices could rise a little."

If consumer demand turns towards consumption it can have an inflationary effect but if part of it goes towards imports, that would help drive demand abroad and counter the appreciating pressure on the rouble.
"With about $23 billion of (gross) reserves, the central bank would be happy to share them with the market," said Aljba-Alliance senior dealer Dmitry Slobodnik.
